product.title: Greek 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Greek: a stress-marked pronunciation guide printed right above every Greek word, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Greek builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of all twenty-four letters, the rules for letter combinations and stress, a summary of articles and noun endings, an A1 verb table, and a glossary. The alphabet is the easy part — and you already know hundreds of Greek words from English. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up: three genders and the article that goes with every noun, the noun ending that changes when it becomes an object, σε fused with the article, the possessive that comes after the noun, and the "like" sentence that turns its subject around.

blocks.text: You already know more Greek than you think. That's not a pep talk — you can count it. *Democracy*, *system*, *program*, *problem*, *theme*, *climate*, *energy*, *atmosphere*, *biology*, *geography*, *history*, *philosophy*, *mathematics*, *physics*, *chemistry*, *technology*, *method*, *period*, *zone*, *museum*, *telephone*, *photography*, *automatic*, *crisis*, *character*, *type*, *drama*, *theater*, *music*, *orchestra*, *machine*: all thirty-one English words in this sentence are Greek words, and nearly all of them are still used in Athens today with almost the same meaning. Even *school*, *church*, *paradise*, and *chair* came from there — through Latin, French, and Old English, but from there all the same.

The only thing standing between you and all those words is the alphabet, and the alphabet is the **easiest** part of the whole journey. Twenty-four letters. One letter, one sound, almost without exception. You already know eleven of them from math and physics class — α, β, γ, δ, ε, θ, λ, μ, π, σ, ω — and most of the rest look exactly like Latin letters. A determined learner can spell out Greek haltingly in one afternoon and read it fluently within a week.

The really hard part lies elsewhere, and this course won't pretend otherwise. Greek sorts **every** noun into one of three genders, requires an **article** in front of nearly all of them — even in front of people's names — and changes the **ending** of the noun and its article according to the word's role in the sentence. In English, "coffee" stays "coffee": *the coffee is hot*, *I want coffee*. In Greek the first is ο καφές and the second τον καφέ. That system — not the letters — is what most often makes beginners give up.

The good news: at A1 you don't need the whole system. You need three genders in just two forms, the present tense, one past tense, one way to talk about the future, and about three hundred words. With that, you can introduce yourself, order food in a ταβέρνα, shop at the market, ask the way in Athens's patternless streets, tell the time, talk about yesterday, and turn down an invitation politely. This course is built so that those forms arrive **one at a time, right after you need them**, not as a six-column table on page three that makes people close the book.

Four things are deliberately done differently here. First, **the pronunciation is printed above each Greek word, with the stressed syllable in CAPITALS**. Stress in Greek isn't decoration: it's written on every word of more than one syllable, and moving it can change the meaning — πότε means "when" while ποτέ means "never". Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** that shows the original structure, even when it sounds odd in English, because that's exactly where the lesson is. Third, the pronunciation guide respells Greek vowels for English readers — **ah, eh, ee, oh, oo** — always short and pure, never gliding as in English *go* or *day*. Fourth, every unit targets **one typical stumbling block**, named openly rather than hidden in a footnote.

Greek has three thousand years of unbroken written history, and Greeks know it. They also know that hardly any foreigners bother to learn it. The first ten words you say correctly in Athens or Thessaloniki will buy you more warmth than a hundred words of English. Καλή αρχή — have a good start.

This course has twenty units. Each unit is designed for one sitting — about twenty to thirty minutes — and contains one dialogue, notes on that dialogue, one to three grammar boxes, vocabulary, four exercises, and their answers. If you do one unit a day, you'll finish in three weeks. Three units a week, in seven weeks. Both are fine; what isn't fine is doing five units in one day and then stopping for a month.
How to work through a unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, only the Greek and the pronunciation.** Don't look at the translation. The goal isn't to understand, but to get your eyes and mouth used to it. Say it out loud — Greek has the sounds δ and θ, which English spells the same way (*th*) but Greek keeps apart, and they will never become easy if you only read silently.
**Read it again with the translation and the literal line.** The literal line is the heart of this course. It shows that *Με λένε Άννα* really says "me they-call Anna", not "my name is Anna".
**Read the notes.** That's where the stumbling blocks mentioned in the foreword are.
**Do the exercises without looking back.** Write by hand if you can; writing Greek letters by hand forces your brain to take each shape apart, and that's what stops you from mixing up ξ and ζ.
**Check against the key, then read the dialogue once more.** The same dialogue will feel different after the exercises.

blocks.title: Three ground rules
items: **Don't skip the next three pages.** The letters, the letter combinations, and stress decide whether your Greek sounds like Greek or like someone spelling out a physics formula.

**Always learn nouns together with their article.** Not *σπίτι*, but **το σπίτι**. Not *καφές*, but **ο καφές**. A noun's gender can almost never be guessed from its meaning, and learning it later means learning everything twice.
**Say it out loud.** Every dialogue, every time. Greek has a very marked rhythm; reading silently loses the stress and flattens your sentences.

front.title: The Greek alphabet: you already know eleven letters

blocks.text: If you've ever sat through a physics or math class, you've already memorized part of this list without noticing. **α** and **β** from the angles of a triangle, **π** from the circumference of a circle, **Δ** for a difference, **λ** for wavelength, **μ** for micro, **σ** for standard deviation, **θ** for an angle of rotation, **Ω** for the unit of resistance, **ε** for epsilon, **γ** from gamma rays. Eleven free letters. Only thirteen to go.

These twenty-four letters have a property that makes Greek far friendlier than English: **almost no silent letters and almost no unexpected spellings**. What you see is what you say. The only complication is that several different letters spell the same sound — η, ι, υ, ει, and οι all sound *ee*. That's a problem for **writing**, not for reading. To read, you never have to guess.
Three piles

items: **Same shape, same sound** (nine): Α α, Ε ε, Ζ ζ, Ι ι, Κ κ, Μ μ, Ν ν, Ο ο, Τ τ. Just read them as usual.

**Same shape, different sound** (four — and this is the trap): **Β β** = **v**, not b. **Η η** = **ee**, not h. **Ρ ρ** = **r**, not p. **Υ υ** = **ee**, not u. These four letters cause most of a beginner's misreadings in the first week.
**New shapes** (eleven): Γ γ, Δ δ, Θ θ, Λ λ, Ξ ξ, Π π, Σ σ ς, Φ φ, Χ χ, Ψ ψ, Ω ω. You've seen most of them in formulas.

blocks.title: Four sounds that need attention
items: **δ** (*dh*) — the *th* in *this*, *that*, *mother*. Tip of the tongue against the upper teeth, vocal cords vibrating. Not d. Ελλάδα = *eh-LAH-**dh**ah*, not "Ellada".
**θ** (*th*) — same place, but without the buzz: *think*, *thanks*. English writes δ and θ with the same *th*; Greek never mixes them. Θεσσαλονίκη = ***th**eh-sah-loh-NEE-kee*.

**γ** (*gh*) — a g that never fully closes, a soft gargle with no English equivalent (like a Spanish g in *lago*). ⚠️ But before the sounds **eh** and **ee**, γ turns into **y** as in *yes*: γεια = *yah*, γυναίκα = *yee-NEH-kah*.
**χ** (*kh*) — like the *ch* in Scottish *loch* or German *Bach*. Before eh and ee it softens into something like a rough *h*, close to German *ich*: χέρι = *KHEH-ree*.

blocks.text: Your first practice needs no book: walk past anything written in Greek — yogurt pots, ship names, club logos — and spell it out letter by letter. The ability to spell comes from boring repetition, not from cleverness.

blocks.title: Σ has two faces
items: **σ** is used at the start and in the middle of a word, **ς** only at the end. One letter, one sound, two shapes — a bit like capital and small letters, except the choice depends on position.
Words that use both at once: **σ**πίτι, φίλο**ς**, Ελλάδα**ς**, κό**σ**μο**ς**.
⚠️ Writing **σ** at the end of a word instantly looks like a foreigner's handwriting. It's the easiest writing mistake to avoid.

front.title: Letter combinations, stress, and two tricky punctuation marks

blocks.text: After the twenty-four letters, one short list remains: pairs of letters read as a single sound. The list is under twelve lines, never changes, and once you know it you can read practically anything.
Vowel pairs
The "hard letters" are θ, κ, ξ, π, σ, τ, φ, χ, ψ. The rule sounds complicated, but your mouth will find it by itself: try saying *avtos* quickly, and the v turns into f on its own.
Consonant pairs

head: Spelling
Sound
Example
rows: **b** at the start of a word, **mb** in the middle
**d** at the start of a word, **nd** in the middle
**g** at the start, **ng** in the middle

blocks.title: ⚠️ Greek has no letters for b and d
items: Β β is already taken for the **v** sound, and Δ δ for the **dh** sound. So when Greek needs to write the sounds **b** and **d** — for loanwords, say — it borrows two letters at once: **μπ** and **ντ**.
That's why *bar* is written **μπαρ**, *Bali* is written **Μπαλί**, *dollar* is written **δολάριο**… but *India* is written **Ινδία** with δ, because that word came in by the old route.
Your own name will most likely be written with μπ or ντ by Greeks. **Bob** → Μπομπ, **David** → Ντέιβιντ. Don't be surprised.

blocks.text: Stress: one mark, one rule, many consequences

Every Greek word of more than one syllable **must** carry one accent mark: ά, έ, ή, ί, ό, ύ, ώ. Never more than one, never fewer, and never further back than the third syllable from the end. Because the mark is always there, you **never have to guess** how to pronounce a new Greek word — unlike English or Russian.

items: ⚠️ **Stress can change the meaning.** πότε (*POH-teh*) = when, ποτέ (*poh-TEH*) = never. πώς (*pohs*) = how, πως (*pohs*) = that. νόμος = law, νομός = prefecture.

⚠️ **Wrong stress makes a word unrecognizable.** Greeks won't try to guess; they'll genuinely not understand. English speakers know the feeling — think *PHOtograph* vs *phoTOgrapher* — but in Greek it happens with every word.
In this course stress is marked with **CAPITAL LETTERS** in the pronunciation, so you don't have to hunt for the little mark above the letter: ευχαριστώ → *ehf-khah-ree-**STOH***.

blocks.text: The question mark shaped like **;** is a little surprise that never stops being funny. A Greek sentence ending in a semicolon isn't trailing off — it's asking.

front.title: Hundreds of Greek words you already know

blocks.text: English has been borrowing from Greek for over a thousand years: through Latin (church and school words), through French (everyday words), and straight from Greek (almost the entire vocabulary of science and medicine). So you start Greek with a few hundred words your ears already know. The table below is only a small sample — all of them are still in everyday use in Greece today.

blocks.title: Four words that traveled a very long way
items: **σχολείο** → Latin *schola* → Old English *scōl* → **school**. The original σχολή meant "leisure": for the ancient Greeks, learning was what you did when you weren't working.
**εκκλησία** → Latin *ecclesia* → French *église*; English keeps it in **ecclesiastical**. It originally meant "an assembly of citizens called together".

**παράδεισος** → Latin *paradisus* → **paradise**. Funnily enough, the word came from Old Persian *paridaida* (walled garden), was borrowed by Greek, and then spread back east through Arabic *firdaus*.
**ευαγγέλιο** *(ehv-ahn-GHEH-lee-oh, "good news")* → Latin *evangelium* → **evangelist**. English *gospel* is a word-for-word translation of it: Old English *gōd spell*, "good news".

blocks.text: ⚠️ Six words whose meaning has shifted

This head start is real, but it has limits: almost all of these are nouns from science or modern life. The words you need most every day — *there is*, *go*, *want*, *big*, *today* — aren't on any such list and must be learned the usual way. Think of this list as a welcome gift, not a shortcut.

back.title: Articles and noun endings on two pages

blocks.text: This page sums up the whole A1 noun system. Don't try to memorize it all at the start — use it as a place to check whenever a form looks unfamiliar. Everything here has already been explained step by step in the units.
Articles

⚠️ Articles are used **far more often** than in English: in front of people's names (ο Γιάννης), country names (η Ελλάδα), nouns used in general (μου αρέσει **ο** καφές — I like coffee), and with possessives (**το** σπίτι μου). Leaving them out is the number-one giveaway of a foreign speaker.
The most common noun endings

blocks.title: Three things that save a lot of memorizing
items: **Neuter nouns never change** between subject and object. A third of all Greek nouns are automatically easier.
**Feminine plural subject and object are identical**: οι ώρες / τις ώρες. Only the article changes.

⚠️ **The -ν of την and τον often drops** in speech and casual writing, unless the next word begins with a vowel or κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, ξ, ψ. When in doubt, just write it in full — it's never considered wrong.

blocks.text: Adjectives follow their noun

back.title: A1 verb forms at a glance

blocks.text: Two verbs to know by heart
Three present-tense verb groups
Because the ending already shows who's doing it, the pronouns **εγώ, εσύ, αυτός** are usually dropped. Use them only for emphasis or contrast: *Εγώ μένω στην Αθήνα, αυτός μένει στη Θεσσαλονίκη.*
The most common past forms (αόριστος)
The endings are always the same for every verb: **-α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν**. So once you know the "I" form, the other five come free: έφαγα, έφαγες, έφαγε, φάγαμε, φάγατε, έφαγαν.
The future and να

items: **θα + one-off form** for a single event: *Αύριο **θα πάω** στην Κρήτη.* — Tomorrow I'll go to Crete.
**θα + present form** for something repeated or ongoing: *Κάθε μέρα **θα πηγαίνω** στη δουλειά.* — Every day I'll be going to work.

⚠️ **Greek has no infinitive.** "I want to go" isn't *θέλω πηγαίνω* but **θέλω να πάω** — literally "I want that I go", with the second verb also changing for the person. The same goes for μπορώ να…, πρέπει να…, ξέρω να…

blocks.text: Numbers

⚠️ The numbers one, three, and four change with the gender of the noun: **ένας** καφές, **μία** μπύρα, **ένα** νερό; **τρεις** μέρες but **τρία** παιδιά; **τέσσερις** ώρες but **τέσσερα** ευρώ. The rest never change.
Time

head: Greek
Say it
Meaning
rows: half past three (literally: three and a half)

blocks.text: ⚠️ *τρεις και μισή* literally "three and a half" means **3:30** — Greek names the hour that has **already passed**, just like English *half past three*. Watch out only if you also speak German or Dutch, where *halb vier* / *half vier* names the **next** hour; that one-hour gap regularly makes people miss appointments.
Days and months

Greek day names are ordinal numbers: Δευτέρα = "second", Τρίτη = "third", Τετάρτη = "fourth", Πέμπτη = "fifth". The count starts from Κυριακή ("the Lord's day") as day one. The month names are almost identical to English — both borrowed them from Latin.

back.title: Pronouns, possessives, question words, and prepositions

blocks.text: Pronouns

⚠️ The possessive stands **after** its noun, and the noun keeps its article: **το** σπίτι **μου** (my house), **η** μητέρα **μου** (my mother), **ο** φίλος **σου** (your friend). If the noun is stressed on the third syllable from the end, it grows a second accent: το όνομ**ά** μου, το αυτοκίνητ**ό** του.
Question words

blocks.text: ⚠️ **σε always fuses with the article that follows.** Never *σε το σπίτι*, always **στο σπίτι**. It's one of the quickest tells between a sentence that sounds Greek and one that sounds translated.
About two hundred of the most frequent words from the twenty units of this course, in English alphabetical order. Nouns are listed with their article — learn them as a pair.

If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you're at a genuine A1 level: you can introduce yourself, order food, shop, ask the way, tell the time, talk about yesterday, and turn down an invitation without sounding rude. That's no small thing. The question now is how to keep going so it doesn't evaporate in three months.
Three next steps

items: **Review the dialogues, not the tables.** Reread the twenty dialogues in this course out loud, one a day, until you can say them without looking. Dialogues that sink in become a stock of ready-made sentences; memorized tables evaporate.
**Move up to A2 through the second past tense (παρατατικός) and conditional sentences.** Those are the two forms you'll miss most once you start telling longer stories.
**Find a listening ear.** Greek has a small number of speakers and online communities that are remarkably kind to beginners. One thirty-minute conversation a week beats three hours of reading alone.

blocks.text: Materials that really help at this level

items: **Songs.** Greece has a song tradition with clear, slow lyrics — look up έντεχνο and ρεμπέτικο. The lyrics are easy to find in writing, and the vocabulary of feelings arrives faster through songs than through word lists.
**News for beginners.** Greek news sites publish short summaries in simple sentences. Read one story a day; don't open the dictionary more than five times per story.
**Menus and signs.** If you get the chance to visit Greece, read every menu from the Greek column first. A menu is the best free vocabulary textbook there is.

blocks.title: The one habit that matters most
items: Say something in Greek **every day**, even if it's just one sentence to yourself. Ten minutes a day beats three hours every Saturday — not because of the total, but because the brain keeps what's repeated often, not what's studied for long.
If you stop for a month, don't start again from Unit 1. Open the last unit you did, read its dialogue out loud, and carry on. Guilt is the most common reason people never come back.

blocks.text: Καλή συνέχεια — keep going. And if one day you're standing in the port of Piraeus, ordering a coffee in Greek, and the reply comes back in Greek without the vendor switching to English — that's the sign this course has done its job.
